newsitem.title: JAPAN: Business halt dents Nomura stock, but loss limited.
newsitem.headline: Business halt dents Nomura stock, but loss limited.

text.p: Scandal-tainted Nomura Securities Co Ltd's shares fell on Wednesday, bruised by news that Japan's securities watchdog filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors against the brokerage on Tuesday evening.

But brokers said further news that Japan's Postal Savings Bureau and the Tokyo metropolitan and Yokohama municipal governments had halted business with Nomura did little additional damage to the shares.

"The market has had time to digest the outcome of the scandal and the possible punitive measures," said Masayuki Matsumoto, Dai-Ichi Securities Co Ltd analyst. "The impact is limited to Nomura, which is well above its 1,100 yen-low posted in the days after the scandal broke, and to the brokerage sector."

Nomura closed down 70 at 1,480 on Wednesday after falling to an intra-day low of 1,460 on trade of 11.22 million shares, the most heavily traded issue on the first section of the bourse. Brokerages were the largest losers on a sector basis.
The closely watched Nikkei average of 225 shares ended higher, however, gaining 80.61 or 0.40 percent to close at 20,209.72.

On Tuesday, Japan's Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) filed a criminal complaint with prosecutors alleging that Nomura, two former executives and a former general manager compensated a client for investment losses.

"Despite its troubles, Nomura is the strongest of the brokerages and will be most able to survive the 'Big Bang' (financial) reforms," said Kunihiro Hatae, Tokyo Securities general manager. "Damage to its share price is likely to be limited."
A dealer at a second-tier brokerage added that if the share prices weaken drastically, bargain-hunting would emerge.

"Many young Nomura employees are saying that if they work hard now, they will achieve success in the company," he said. "Nomura could stage a dramatic comeback so it's better to buy the share when it falls."
